newsitem.title: USA: Fed expected to opt to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Fed expected to opt to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to decide on Wednesday to hold interest rates steady as the economy remains remarkably free of inflation nearly six years into an expansion, analysts said.

Many analysts, though, believe it is only a matter of time before the central bank tightens credit. With the job market taut and wages picking up, they said the Fed will eventually need to raise rates to keep inflation in check.

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee resumed its meeting at 9:00 a.m. 1400 GMT on Wednesday after spending the previous afternoon discussing the economy. An announcement on rates is expected at about 2:15 p.m. 1915 GMT.
The Fed has held rates steady for over a year, since cutting them by a quarter percentage point on Jan. 31, 1996.
The federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for loans now stands at 5.25 percent. The discount rate the Fed charges on its loans to the banks is 5 percent.
U.S. stock and bond prices rose in early trading on Wednesday, partly on hopes the Fed will hold rates steady.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told state governors on Sunday he saw no evidence of significant price pressures in the economy, Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad said.
"He gave a positive report. We've had growth with low inflation," Branstad told reporters after the governors' closed-door meeting with the Fed chief.

The economy ended 1996 with a bang, growing at a 4.7 percent annualized rate in the final three months of the year. That was more than double the pace of the previous quarter and the fastest rate of growth in 2-1/2 years.
But inflation remained benign. The implicit price deflator that measures price changes rose a mere 1.4 percent rate in the fourth quarter, the slowest pace since 1967.

In a sign that the economy may be about to slow down from its torrid fourth-quarter pace, the government reported on Wednesday that factory orders fell by 1.3 percent in December, mainly because of weaker demand for electronic equipment.
"The economy has retained considerable vigour, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," Greenspan told lawmakers last month.
But he also warned of the risk of higher inflation in the future and said the Fed needed to be ready to act to contain price pressures once they started to show signs of building.

At their meeting this week, Fed policy-makers were also scheduled to discuss their projections for economic growth, inflation and unemployment this year for presentation by Greenspan to Congress later this month.

Several Fed policy-makers have already said publicly that they expect moderate economic growth this year in the two to 2-1/2 percent range. On a fourth-quarter-on-fourth-quarter basis, the economy grew by 3.4 percent last year.

But Chris Varvares, President of Macroeconomic Advisers of St. Louis, said there is a risk that inflation will pick up this year even if growth moderates because the economy is already running at such a high level of capacity.

That eventually may prove enough to convince the Fed to take out some "monetary insurance" and raise interest rates a notch. But that will not happen until it can get a better reading of where the economy -- and inflation -- is headed, he said.
